title: Dark patterns: confirmshaming, roach motels and preselected consent
description: Nineteen interfaces built to work against the person using them. Every question shows a design as a mockup and asks what it is doing; every explanation shows the same screen redesigned honestly. Covers confirmshaming, pre-ticked consent, cancellation flows that run four pages deep, countdown timers that reset on reload, fees that arrive one screen at a time, and pricing tables that resist comparison, alongside what the GDPR asks of a consent box, what the FTC found inside Amazon's cancellation flow, and how the EU Digital Services Act names the harm.
author: Quizbun

questions.title: This pop-up offers a discount, and the link that declines it reads *No thanks, I like paying full price.* What makes that wording a deceptive pattern rather than ordinary sales copy?

images.alt: A newsletter pop-up headed 'Before you go…' offering 20% off a first order. It has an email field and a large blue button reading 'Yes, save me 20%'. Underneath, in small pale grey underlined text, sits the only way to decline: 'No thanks, I like paying full price.'
The same pop-up with two buttons of equal size side by side: a blue 'Get 20% off' and an outlined 'No thanks'. A line underneath reads 'One email a week. Unsubscribe in one click.'
images.caption: The same offer with the judgement taken out. Both answers get a real button, and the small print says what subscribing means.

options.text: The decline label describes the person rather than the choice, so refusing costs a small hit to self-image on top of losing the discount.
Trading a discount for an email address is the manipulation, whatever the buttons happen to say.
The discount is genuine but time-limited, and the pop-up never says when it runs out.
The pop-up blocks the page, and blocking the page is what makes any modal deceptive.

questions.explanation:
Confirmshaming works on the label of the refusal. `Yes, save me 20%` and `No thanks, I like paying full price` lead to the same two outcomes, but the second one asks you to say something about yourself to get there.

The pressure is small and it is deliberate. Declining now carries a private cost, so some people take the discount to avoid the sentence rather than because they want the emails. A subscriber list built that way tells the shop nothing about who actually wanted to hear from it.

The redesign keeps the offer and drops the judgement. Both answers get a real button, both labels name the outcome, and the line underneath says what subscribing involves.

questions.title: A delete dialog says *Deleting this project also deletes 3 years of build history. This cannot be undone.* Why is that not confirmshaming, even though it is written to make you hesitate?

options.text: It states a consequence the user needs before deciding. Confirmshaming adds no information and attaches a judgement to the person choosing instead.
It sits in a delete flow, and destructive actions are exempt from the rules on deceptive design.
It is confirmshaming, of the kind regulators tolerate because the wording is factual.
Confirmshaming applies only to marketing consent, so nothing outside a consent flow can qualify.

questions.explanation:
Friction is not the test. Plenty of good interfaces slow you down on purpose, because a decision with permanent consequences deserves a pause.

The test is what the extra words do. `3 years of build history` is a fact you need and probably do not have in your head. `I like paying full price` is not a fact about the price, the offer, or anything else on the screen. It is a sentence about you, and it exists to make declining feel worse.

Here is a practical check for reviewing copy. Strike out every clause that carries no information. If the warning still reads as complete, the copy was doing its job. If what you struck out was the whole persuasive force, it was shaming.

questions.title: The marketing and data-sharing boxes on this sign-up form arrive already ticked, and nothing stops the user unticking either one. Under the GDPR, why can a tick that arrives that way still fail as consent?

images.alt: A 'Create your account' form with email and password fields. Below them, three checkboxes: 'Send me product news and offers' and 'Share my details with selected partners' are both already ticked, while 'I agree to the Terms of Service' is empty. A blue 'Create account' button sits underneath.

The same form with three empty checkboxes: 'Email me product announcements', 'Email me offers from our partners', and, below a dividing line, 'I agree to the Terms of Service'. A note reads 'Both are optional. Change them any time in Settings.'
images.caption: Every box starts empty, each purpose is asked separately, and the contractual agreement is separated from the optional marketing.

options.text: Consent has to be an unambiguous indication given by a clear affirmative act, and leaving a box as you found it is not an act at all.
Pre-ticked boxes are acceptable as long as the form explains what each one does before the user submits it.
They fail only where the site cannot demonstrate that the user actually read the label.
They are valid consent, provided the site lets the user withdraw it later in the same number of clicks.

questions.explanation:
Article 4(11) defines consent as a freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous indication of the person's wishes, given by a statement or by a clear affirmative action. Recital 32 spells out what fails that bar: silence, pre-ticked boxes, and inactivity.

The Court of Justice settled the point in *Planet49* on 1 October 2019. A pre-ticked cookie box cannot be valid consent, because an untouched box cannot tell you whether the person agreed, skimmed past it, or never saw it. Consent has to leave evidence, and inaction leaves none.

The redesign asks the same three questions and changes what a tick means. Every box starts empty, each purpose is asked on its own so a yes to one is not a yes to all, and the contractual agreement sits apart from the optional marketing.
questions.references: [GDPR: Article 4(11), definition of consent](https://gdpr-info.eu/art-4-gdpr/) · [GDPR: Recital 32, conditions for consent](https://gdpr-info.eu/recitals/no-32/) · [CJEU: Planet49, Case C-673/17](https://curia.europa.eu/juris/liste.jsf?num=C-673/17)

questions.title: A consent panel lists 412 advertising partners, each with its own switch, next to a single large *Accept all*. Which of the EDPB's categories does this fit, and what is the mechanism?

images.alt: A 'Manage your preferences' panel open on a 'Legitimate interest (412)' tab. Four named advertising companies are listed, each with a switch already turned on, above the line '… and 408 more, each with its own switch'. A small grey 'Save preferences' button sits bottom left and a large blue 'Accept all' button bottom right. There is no reject button.

The same panel rebuilt around four purposes rather than companies: storing information on the device, personalised advertising, audience measurement, and product development. Every switch is off. Two buttons of equal size read 'Reject all' and 'Accept all', with a smaller 'Save' beside them.
images.caption: Four purposes instead of 412 companies, and refusing now costs the same single click as accepting.

options.text: Overloading. The effort of refusing grows with the number of partners while accepting stays at one click, so fatigue produces the yes.
Skipping. The panel is built so that users never stop to think about their data at all.
Nagging. The same panel returns on every page until the user gives in and accepts.
Stirring. The size and colour of *Accept all* work on emotion rather than on reason.

questions.explanation:
The EDPB sorts deceptive design into six families: Overloading, Skipping, Stirring, Obstructing, Fickle, and Left in the Dark. Overloading is the one that works by volume. Give someone more requests, options or text than the decision is worth and they take the shortcut.

Count the interactions. Accepting costs one. Refusing costs 412, and the switches sit under a *Legitimate interest* tab that starts on. That tab is a second problem: storing or reading information on someone's device needs consent under the ePrivacy Directive, and legitimate interest is not an alternative route to it.

The redesign works because it changes the unit. Nobody has an opinion about Adloox SA, they have an opinion about being profiled, so ask about the four purposes rather than the 412 companies. Then `Reject all` and `Accept all` cost the same single click.

questions.title: In January 2022 the French regulator announced fines of €150 million against Google and €60 million against Facebook over banners shaped like this one. What did it find unlawful?

images.alt: A browser window with an article behind a cookie banner headed 'We value your privacy', explaining that the site and 412 partners want to store and access information on the device. A large blue 'Accept all' button dominates the right side. The only alternative is the words 'Manage options' in tiny, very pale text in the bottom left corner.

The same banner with the same wording. 'Reject all' and 'Accept all' now sit stacked in the same position, at the same size, one outlined and one filled. 'Manage options' appears as a normal, legible link.
images.caption: Same banner, same wording, same partners. Only the cost of refusing changed.

options.text: Accepting took one click while refusing took several, and that imbalance steers people toward consent, so the consent was not freely given.
The banner named 412 partners without linking to the privacy policy of each one.
Cookies were written to the device before the visitor interacted with the banner at all.
The banner covered part of the article, which counts as obstructing access to the service.

questions.explanation:
The CNIL's decisions, taken on 31 December 2021 and announced on 6 January 2022, turned on a click count. On facebook.com, google.fr and youtube.com a single button accepted every cookie, and no equivalent button refused them. Refusal was reachable, but only through several further steps.

The reasoning matters more than the sums. Consent has to be freely given, and a choice is not free when one branch is cheap and the other is expensive. Both companies were ordered to give users in France a refusal as simple as the acceptance within three months, on pain of €100,000 for every further day.

Look at the redesign and notice what did not change. Same banner, same wording, same 412 partners. `Reject all` simply became a button of the same size in the same place, and `Manage options` became legible.
questions.references: [TechCrunch: France fines Google and Facebook over cookie consent dark patterns](https://techcrunch.com/2022/01/06/cnil-facebook-google-cookie-consent-eprivacy-breaches/) · [Deceptive Patterns: Visual interference](https://www.deceptive.design/types/visual-interference)

questions.title: Cheap to enter and laborious to leave: which name did the original dark-patterns taxonomy give this shape, borrowing it from a 1970s insect-trap slogan about checking in and never checking out?
questions.description: Two words. The taxonomy has since renamed it.
questions.explanation:
Harry Brignull's 2010 taxonomy called it the roach motel, after the Black Flag trap sold with the line *Roaches check in, but they don't check out*. The site that hosts that taxonomy now calls the same shape *Hard to cancel*, because regulators needed a name they could put in a decision.

The pattern is asymmetry rather than difficulty. Nobody objects to a cancellation that takes two clicks when signing up took two. The problem appears when signing up takes one click on the web and cancelling takes a phone call during business hours.

In the United States, ROSCA has required simple cancellation mechanisms for online negative-option sales since 2010. The FTC's more specific click-to-cancel rule was finalised in 2024 and then vacated by the Eighth Circuit in July 2025 over a skipped regulatory analysis, so a fresh rulemaking is under way. The underlying obligation never went anywhere.

questions.title: Signing up for Amazon Prime took one click. The FTC's 2023 complaint described a cancellation flow that Amazon had named after Homer's epic. How many clicks did the complaint say cancelling took?
questions.description: Answer with the number only, for example `3`.

images.alt: Two flows compared. Subscribing is one box, 'Start free trial, 1 click', leading straight to 'Subscribed'. Cancelling is four red boxes in a row: 'Account, find the setting', 'Are you sure? remind me later', 'Your benefits, pause instead', and 'Confirm, yes cancel'. A line below reads '4 pages, 6 clicks, 15 options, every one of them a chance to give up'.
images.caption: The asymmetry described in the FTC's complaint: one click in, six clicks and four pages out.

images.alt: Three green boxes in a row: 'Account, cancel membership', 'Confirm, access ends 14 March', and 'Cancelled, confirmation emailed'. A line below reads 'Same page you subscribed on, 2 clicks, no retention maze'.
images.caption: The same job done symmetrically, on the page where the subscription started.

questions.explanation:
Six clicks across four pages, with fifteen options along the way. Amazon called the flow Iliad internally, which tells you the length was understood in-house.

Every screen was a chance to stop: your Prime *journey*, the benefits you were about to lose, a discount, `Remind Me Later`, `Keep My Membership`. None of those are lies. They work by putting the exit behind a sequence of opportunities to change your mind, and enough people give up somewhere in the middle for the sequence to pay for itself.

Amazon settled in September 2025 for $2.5 billion: a $1 billion civil penalty, the largest ever imposed for an FTC rule violation, plus $1.5 billion in refunds, and an order to change how Prime is entered and left.

The fix costs nothing technically. Put `Cancel membership` on the account page, confirm once, state the date access ends, and send an email.
questions.references: [FTC: Historic $2.5 billion settlement against Amazon](https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2025/09/ftc-secures-historic-25-billion-settlement-against-amazon) · [FTC v. Amazon.com, Inc. (ROSCA)](https://www.ftc.gov/legal-library/browse/cases-proceedings/2123050-amazoncom-inc-rosca-ftc-v)

questions.title: Which of these changes actually fix a subscription that is harder to leave than it was to join?

options.text: Putting the cancellation control in the same interface used to subscribe, so a sign-up on the web can be cancelled on the web.
Confirming the cancellation on screen and by email, stating the date access ends.
Letting a retention offer appear at most once, dismissible by the same click that continues the cancellation.
Replacing the online cancellation with a phone line staffed during business hours.
Keeping the existing flow and adding a page that sets out the cancellation policy in full.
Emailing former subscribers a month later to ask them to reconsider.

questions.explanation:
There is a measurable test for this, and it does not need a lawyer. Count the steps from a logged-in state to a completed sign-up, then count the steps from a logged-in state to a completed cancellation. If the second number is much larger, the design has an answer to give.

That is why the first three changes work and the others do not. Same channel, one confirmation, one retention offer that costs nothing to refuse. A phone line instead of a web flow makes the asymmetry worse, and it is precisely what ROSCA's requirement of a simple cancellation mechanism was written about. A policy page adds reading without removing steps. A reconsideration email is a different pattern, nagging, arriving after the user has already decided.

Explaining the maze is not the same as removing it.

questions.title: A product page shows a countdown labelled *Offer ends in 04:59*. Which observation across these three visits proves the deadline is manufactured?

images.alt: A product card for an Alpine down jacket at £129.00, reduced from £159.00, beside a red panel reading 'Offer ends in 04:59'. Below, under the heading 'The same product page, three separate visits', three small browser windows are shown: Tuesday 10:02 on a first visit, Tuesday 10:07 after a reload, and Wednesday 08:15 in a new private window. All three display 04:59.

The same product card, with the red countdown replaced by a green panel reading 'Sale price held until Sun 23 March, 23:59 GMT'. Lines below note that the deadline is a date, so every visitor sees the same one and a reload does not move it, and that the price returns to £159.00 on 24 March.
images.caption: A deadline anyone can hold the shop to: a fixed date, and the price it returns to.

options.text: It reads 04:59 on a reload five minutes later and again the next morning, so it counts down from page load rather than toward a fixed moment.
The countdown is under five minutes, and no genuine sale would ever run on a clock that short.
The old price appears next to the new one, which means the discount is not real either.
The timer is red, and red is the standard signal of a manufactured deadline.

questions.explanation:
A real deadline is a point in time. It is the same instant for everyone looking at the page, so it survives a reload, a different browser, and a night's sleep. The clock across these three visits does none of that. It starts at five minutes whenever the page loads, which makes it a stopwatch dressed as a deadline.

The test is cheap and it works anywhere. Reload the page, or open it in a private window. If the number resets, the pressure was manufactured.

Real deadlines survive being written down. The honest version puts the end of the sale on the page as a date and a time, and says what the price returns to afterwards.
questions.references: [Deceptive Patterns: Fake urgency](https://www.deceptive.design/types/fake-urgency) · [Mathur et al.: Dark Patterns at Scale (CSCW 2019)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.07032)

questions.title: *Only 2 left in stock* appears under a product. What has to be true for that line to be an honest signal rather than fake scarcity?

options.text: It is read from the same inventory count the warehouse works from, and it moves as stock moves, including upward after a restock.
It is true of at least one warehouse somewhere in the fulfilment network.
A footnote elsewhere on the site explains that stock figures are approximate.
It is shown only to visitors who have already added the item to a basket, so it cannot colour a first impression.

questions.explanation:
Scarcity is real. Shops run out, and telling a shopper that two are left on the shelf is information they would want.

Fake scarcity is a number cut loose from the thing it claims to measure. Mathur and colleagues crawled roughly 11,000 shopping sites for their CSCW 2019 paper and found 1,818 instances of deceptive design across fifteen types and seven categories. Low-stock and high-demand messages were among them, including counts that turned out to be hardcoded or randomised.

Two checks separate the two. A real count moves in both directions, because restocking happens. And a real count is the figure the warehouse system holds, not one computed in the page to make you hurry.
questions.references: [Mathur et al.: Dark Patterns at Scale, a Crawl of 11K Shopping Websites](https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.07032) · [Deceptive Patterns: Fake scarcity](https://www.deceptive.design/types/fake-scarcity)

questions.title: Two tickets are advertised at £48.00 each. The service fee is £12.50 per ticket, order processing is £6.00 and delivery is £4.00. What does the order actually cost, in pounds?
questions.description: Answer with the number only, for example `84.50`.

images.alt: Four checkout screens in a row under the heading 'One purchase, four screens, and a total you never see until the end'. Search results show £48.00 per ticket and the note 'the advertised price'. Choose seats shows 2 × £48.00 and 'still no fees'. Delivery adds a service fee of £12.50 per ticket, 'first fee appears'. Payment adds order processing £6.00 and delivery £4.00, with 'Total: after card details' and the note 'two more fees'.

A single listing reading 'Alpine Festival, Saturday, 2 tickets' above a large '£65.50 per ticket, every fee included'. A breakdown lists ticket £48.00, service fee £12.50, order processing £3.00 and delivery £2.00, with a total for 2 tickets of £131.00 and the note 'The number in the search results is the number you pay.'
images.caption: All-in pricing does not remove the fees, it moves them to the front. The breakdown is still there for anyone who wants it.

questions.explanation:
£96.00 for the tickets, £25.00 in service fees, £6.00 to process the order and £4.00 to deliver it. £131.00, which is 36% above the price that got you to click.

Drip pricing works on the order the numbers arrive in. The advertised £48.00 sets the anchor and does the comparing against other sites. Every fee after that is judged against a decision you have already taken, and by the payment screen you have chosen seats and typed card details you would have to redo somewhere else. Gabaix and Laibson modelled this in 2006: in a market where some buyers never look past the headline price, hiding the add-ons is the profitable move even under fierce competition.

All-in pricing does not remove the fees. It moves them. The search result reads £65.50 per ticket, the breakdown stays available, and the first number you see is the one you pay.
questions.references: [Gabaix & Laibson: Shrouded Attributes, Consumer Myopia, and Information Suppression in Competitive Markets (NBER, 2005)](https://www.nber.org/papers/w11755) · [Deceptive Patterns: Hidden costs](https://www.deceptive.design/types/hidden-costs)

questions.title: A basket contains *Shipping Protection, £4.99*, which the shopper never chose. What separates this from an ordinary upsell?

images.alt: A basket showing a Merino crew sweater at £89.00 and, styled like a second product, a line reading 'Shipping Protection, Added to your order, £4.99' with its switch already on and a faint 'Remove' label beside it. The subtotal reads £93.99.

The same basket with the sweater at £89.00 and, below it, an empty checkbox reading 'Add shipping protection for £4.99' with the note 'Covers loss or damage in transit. Nothing is added until you tick it.' The order total reads £89.00.
images.caption: Same product, same price, same explanation. The only change is what happens when the shopper does nothing.

options.text: The site put it in the basket and left it switched on, so the shopper pays unless they notice and act. An upsell asks, and costs nothing if it is ignored.
The price. An add-on under £5 counts as sneaking, while larger ones count as upsells.
The wording. Calling it *protection* rather than *insurance* is what makes the line deceptive.
Nothing separates them. Any add-on presented inside a basket is a deceptive pattern.

questions.explanation:
Sneaking is the category, and the default is the mechanism. Two designs offer the same product at the same price, and the only difference is what happens when the shopper does nothing. One collects £4.99, the other collects nothing.

That difference is not small. Defaults carry enormous weight, because doing nothing is easy and reversing a decision takes attention nobody is spending on a basket page.

The redesign gives up the revenue that comes from inattention and keeps the revenue that comes from wanting the thing. Same product, same price, same explanation of what it covers, an empty box, and a total that matches what the shopper picked.
questions.references: [Deceptive Patterns: Sneaking](https://www.deceptive.design/types/sneaking) · [Johnson & Goldstein: Do Defaults Save Lives? (Science, 2003)](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1091721)

questions.title: These three email settings point in different directions. Which combination results in no email at all?

images.alt: An 'Email preferences' card with three checkboxes. Empty: 'Do not send me marketing email.' Ticked: 'Untick this box if you would rather not hear from our partners.' Ticked: 'Send me the weekly digest.' A 'Save preferences' button sits below.

The same card rebuilt under the heading 'Send me:' with three empty checkboxes reading 'Product announcements', 'Offers from our partners' and 'The weekly digest'. A note reads 'Every box points the same way: ticked means yes. All three start empty.'
images.caption: One rule for all three boxes, and a reader who ticks nothing has said no to everything.

options.text: Tick *Do not send me marketing email*, and clear the other two.
Clear all three.
Tick all three.
Leave the form exactly as it arrived. The defaults already send nothing.

questions.explanation:
The first row is a negative statement you agree with by ticking. The second is an instruction about the box itself, wrapped around a second negative. The third is a plain positive. Getting to silence means holding three different mappings between a tick and an outcome in your head at once.

Trick wording needs no lie. Every label here is accurate. The work has been moved onto the reader, and the reader is skimming a form on the way to something else, so the mistakes fall in a direction that suits the sender.

One rule fixes it. A tick means yes to the thing named, every time, and the boxes start empty. Then the form is legible at a glance.
questions.references: [Deceptive Patterns: Trick wording](https://www.deceptive.design/types/trick-wording) · [EDPB: Guidelines 03/2022 on deceptive design patterns](https://www.edpb.europa.eu/our-work-tools/our-documents/guidelines/guidelines-032022-deceptive-design-patterns-social-media_en)

questions.title: Three plans are priced per user per month, per user per year, and per seat per day. Which one actually costs the least per user per month?

images.alt: Three pricing cards. Starter: $9 per user per month, billed annually, with 'Up to 5 collaborators', '2 GB storage' and 'Email support'. Growth, outlined in blue under a 'Most popular' badge: $132 per user per year, billed annually, with 'Team size: small', 'Storage: generous' and 'Priority support'. Scale: $0.42 per seat per day, billed monthly, with 'Unlimited seats*', '500 GB pooled' and '24/7 support'.

The same three plans converted to one unit: Starter $9.00, Growth $11.00 and Scale $12.78 per user per month, each showing its original phrasing underneath. The feature rows now use identical wording in the same order. Starter carries a small green 'cheapest' tag and no plan is highlighted.
images.caption: One unit, one vocabulary, no badge steering the eye. Starter is cheapest, and the design no longer hides it.

options.text: Starter, at $9.00.
Growth, at $11.00, which is also the plan marked *Most popular*.
Scale. A daily seat rate is billed only for days a seat is used, which works out lowest for most teams.
The page does not carry enough information to work it out.

questions.explanation:
Converted into one unit the plans are $9.00, $11.00 and about $12.78 per user per month. Starter is the cheapest, and it is the only one of the three without a badge.

Comparison prevention does not hide the prices. All three are printed in full. What it hides is the comparison, by asking you to do arithmetic across three denominators while you are trying to choose. Most people do not, and the eye falls back on the one cue that is doing no arithmetic at all: the blue border and the *Most popular* label.

The honest page states one unit for all three, repeats the original phrasing underneath so nothing is lost, and describes the same feature with the same words so the rows line up. Then the comparison is free, and the badge is not needed to make the choice for you.

questions.title: A download page shows three large *DOWNLOAD* buttons and, lower down, a plain text link. Which signal reliably identifies the file the page is actually about?

images.alt: A download page headed 'sqlite-tools-3.45.1.zip'. Three identical large green buttons read 'DOWNLOAD, start now · free', each with a tiny low-contrast 'Ad' marker in its top right corner. Below a dividing line, under the heading 'Files', a plain blue link reads 'sqlite-tools-3.45.1.zip (2.1 MB)', followed by links to a checksum and the source archive.

The same page rebuilt. One blue button reads 'Download sqlite-tools-3.45.1.zip (2.1 MB)', with a SHA-256 line and a release date below it. To the right, a dashed box clearly headed 'Advertisement' holds placeholder text, a 'Learn more' control and the line 'Paid placement, not part of this site'.
images.caption: The real download becomes the most prominent thing on the page and says what it is. The advertisement gets a border and a legible label.

options.text: The element that names the exact filename and its size, because the site knows both and an advertiser does not.
The most prominent control, because a site puts its own action first.
Whichever button carries no *Ad* marker, because disclosure is required on every advertisement.
The green button, because on download pages green is the convention for the real file.

questions.explanation:
Ad networks buy the space, not the content. An advertiser writes `DOWNLOAD` because that word wins clicks on pages like this one, and it cannot write `sqlite-tools-3.45.1.zip (2.1 MB)` because it has no idea what the page is about. That asymmetry is the reliable signal, and it holds whatever the buttons look like.

The disclosures are usually there, at seven pixels, in low contrast, in a corner. Present and unreadable is the design: the marker satisfies the requirement while the layout defeats it.

The honest page inverts the hierarchy. The real download is the largest element and it names the file. The advertisement gets a border, a legible label, and a visual style nobody could mistake for a control belonging to the site.

questions.title: A notification prompt offers *Allow* and *Not now*, and comes back on every visit. Which property of that pair of buttons makes it nagging?

images.alt: A dialog asking 'Turn on notifications?' with the line 'Never miss an order update, a price drop or a story picked for you', a blue 'Allow' button and a grey 'Not now' button. Below it, three smaller copies of the same dialog are labelled Visit 2, Visit 3 and Visit 4, each offering the same two answers.

The same dialog with three answers instead of two: 'Allow', 'Not now' and an outlined 'Never'. The body reads 'We will tell you when this order ships. Nothing else, and you can switch it off later.' Notes below say it is asked once, straight after an order is placed, and that 'Never' is stored so the prompt does not come back.
images.caption: A refusal that is remembered, asked at the moment when the answer is obvious.

options.text: Only one of the two answers is recorded. *Allow* is final while *Not now* expires, so refusing is paid for on every visit and accepting is paid for once.
The prompt arrives before the user has done anything that would need notifications.
*Allow* is the primary button and *Not now* is not, which is visual interference.
The prompt interrupts the page, and interrupting the page is what nagging means.

questions.explanation:
Gray and colleagues named nagging in their 2018 CHI study of deceptive design: a repeated interruption that pulls the user away from what they were doing. What makes this particular prompt nagging is the wording of its buttons.

*Not now* is a postponement, not an answer, and it is the only refusal offered. So the two branches are not symmetric over time. Say yes once and you are finished. Say no and you will be asked again, and again, and eventually the arithmetic favours giving in for reasons that have nothing to do with wanting notifications.

Two changes fix it. Offer a refusal that is remembered, and ask at a moment when the answer is obvious. A prompt that arrives right after an order, offering to say when it ships, gets an honest yes or an honest no. A prompt that arrives on page load gets a reflex.
questions.references: [Gray, Kou, Battles, Hoggatt & Toombs: The Dark (Patterns) Side of UX Design (CHI 2018)](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3173574.3174108) · [Deceptive Patterns: Nagging](https://www.deceptive.design/types/nagging)

questions.title: Every form has to default to something, and most people accept whatever it defaults to. Which of these defaults survive scrutiny?

options.text: Organ donor registration set to opt out by law, reversible at any time in one step, with nothing gained by whoever built the form.
A privacy setting that starts at its most protective value, which is what the GDPR requires by default.
Automatic enrolment into a workplace pension, with a documented opt-out the employer has to honour.
A marketing checkbox that arrives ticked on a sign-up form.
*Save my card for future purchases*, pre-selected at the checkout.
A free trial that rolls into an annual plan with no reminder before the charge lands.

questions.explanation:
There is no neutral default. Whatever the box starts as, most people will leave it there, so the design has already made a choice on their behalf. The question is which choice, and for whose benefit.

Johnson and Goldstein published the sharpest demonstration in *Science* in 2003. Consent to organ donation ran below 30% in several opt-in countries and above 85% in comparable opt-out ones. Same populations, same values, different form.

Three questions separate a defensible default from a deceptive one. Who gains when the user does nothing? How expensive is it to change? And does the law treat this particular choice as consent, since the GDPR does not accept a pre-ticked box as consent no matter who benefits. The pension and the privacy setting pass all three. The ticked marketing box fails the first and the third.
questions.references: [Johnson & Goldstein: Do Defaults Save Lives? (Science, 2003)](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1091721) · [GDPR: Article 25, data protection by design and by default](https://gdpr-info.eu/art-25-gdpr/)

questions.title: Article 25 of the EU Digital Services Act addresses deceptive interfaces directly. What does it prohibit?

options.text: Designing, organising or operating an online interface in a way that deceives or manipulates users, or otherwise materially distorts or impairs their ability to make free and informed decisions.
Collecting personal data through an interface without a lawful basis, which is the obligation the GDPR already imposes.
Showing personalised advertising to anyone who has not consented through a separate standalone dialog.
Any interface element a user reports as confusing, once a national regulator has upheld the report.

questions.explanation:
The wording is broad on purpose. It does not list patterns, it names the harm: an interface that distorts your ability to decide. Recital 67 supplies the examples, among them choices presented in a non-neutral way, requests repeated after the user has already answered, and making a service harder to leave than to join.

Two details are worth carrying around. The obligation has applied to online platforms since 17 February 2024, and it reaches beyond the very large platforms designated under Article 33, though Article 19 exempts micro and small enterprises. And it sits alongside the GDPR rather than replacing it. Consent rules govern the data, Article 25 governs the interface, and a single banner can breach both.

This is also why *deceptive design* is displacing *dark patterns* as the term of art. Regulators wanted a name that describes what the design does, and the EDPB and the DSA both moved to that language.

questions.title: The EDPB sorts deceptive design into Overloading, Skipping, Stirring, Obstructing, Fickle and Left in the Dark. Which interface belongs to *Left in the Dark*?

options.text: A privacy setting that exists but sits where users will not find it, with nothing to explain what turning it on would change.
A cancellation flow that puts a retention offer on every step, so leaving takes longer than joining did.
A consent panel that lists every partner separately, so refusing takes hundreds of interactions.
A settings page where the delete control appears in a different place each time it loads.

questions.explanation:
Left in the Dark covers interfaces that hide information or controls, or leave people unsure how their data is being processed. A control can exist and still fail the test, because a setting nobody can find is not a setting anybody can use.

The other three describe real categories too. Putting a retention offer on every step is Obstructing. Listing every partner separately is Overloading. A control that moves between page loads is Fickle. Stirring is the emotional one, which is where confirmshaming lives, and Skipping is designing a flow so the data question never gets considered at all.

Naming the mechanism is what makes a design review actionable. *This feels manipulative* starts an argument. *Refusing costs 412 interactions and accepting costs one* names a number somebody can change.
questions.references: [EDPB: Guidelines 03/2022 on deceptive design patterns in social media platform interfaces](https://www.edpb.europa.eu/our-work-tools/our-documents/guidelines/guidelines-032022-deceptive-design-patterns-social-media_en)
